questions.q: What happens, in practice, when a pipeline fails the build on every scan finding regardless of severity?
options: Nothing changes -- build times stay the same and developers stay fully engaged
Developers learn to tune the pipeline out, finding ways around it rather than trusting it, so the gate stops functioning as a real gate
The scanners automatically adjust their own thresholds
Security findings disappear because the build simply won't run
questions.explain: The lesson describes how blocking on every finding, regardless of severity, teaches developers to route around the gate -- via suppressions, disabling checks, or ignoring failures -- until it no longer functions as a meaningful gate.

questions.q: In the severity-based gate design this lesson recommends, what happens to Medium-severity findings?
options: They are deleted automatically without review
They are escalated directly to company leadership
They fail the build exactly like Critical and High findings
They surface as a warning or ticket for later triage, but do not block the merge
questions.explain: The lesson's design has Critical and High findings block the build, while Medium findings surface as a non-blocking warning for the team to triage on its own schedule.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend a "baseline" when turning on a scanner for the first time against an existing codebase?
options: A baseline prevents pre-existing findings from blocking every team's next unrelated pull request, by having the gate fail only on genuinely new findings
A baseline is required by law for all security scanners
A baseline permanently disables the scanner going forward
A baseline automatically fixes all pre-existing vulnerabilities
questions.explain: Without a baseline, a first-time scan's backlog of pre-existing findings would block every subsequent pull request; a baseline lets the gate fire only on new findings introduced after rollout.

questions.q: In the example gate script shown in this lesson, why does the scan step itself use `|| true` instead of letting the scan command fail the job directly?
options: So that the scan results are deleted before anyone can read them
Because pip-audit cannot be run inside GitHub Actions otherwise
So that a separate evaluation step can read the structured scan output and make the actual pass/fail decision based on severity
So that the build always passes no matter what the scan finds
questions.explain: Separating the scan from the decision lets the severity-based evaluation step decide pass or fail consistently, instead of having the scan tool's own exit code dictate the outcome.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about a security gate's severity thresholds over time?
options: They should never be changed once set, to avoid any inconsistency
Teams revisit and tune them as they learn which finding categories matter, so that a failed build continues to mean something real developers will act on
They are a one-time decision made before the pipeline first runs and never revisited
They are set entirely by the scanning tool vendor and cannot be adjusted
questions.explain: The lesson frames gate thresholds as something teams tune over time, keeping the goal that a failed build should mean something real, so developers fix it instead of routing around it.
